Three feet.

LaneSaber is an LED safety pole that mounts to your rear rack and swings out to mark the legal 3-foot passing distance, so a driver can see exactly where the line is before they cross it. The plans and print files are free, and honestly? We'd rather you built your own. It now comes in two versions: the metal original, and V2, the 3D printed one.

The incentive is to build it yourself

That's the whole model. The plans and 3D print files cost nothing. The printed pieces can come off any 3D printer. Find one in your neighborhood, at your local library, or at a makerspace; most libraries print for the cost of filament. The pole is a hardware-store driveway marker. You can order parts from us if you get stuck, and the kits keep the project alive, but we'd genuinely rather you made your own, or your co-op made twenty. Every LaneSaber built locally is one less package shipped and one more town covered.

It talks to drivers so you don't have to

Most close passes aren't malice. Drivers genuinely can't judge where your space ends. LaneSaber replaces shouting and guesswork with a bright, physical line they can see. Non-verbal, unambiguous, and nothing about it can hurt a car or a rider: the end is soft and rubber-covered, the pole is floppy fiberglass, and if it's ever hit hard, it snaps instead of spearing.

Vertical while you ride

Pole up, you're a follow-the-leader marker: group rides, Bike Bus leaders, and Bike Party sweeps use it as a totem everyone can spot.

Horizontal when it counts

Flip it out to the left and it draws the 3-foot line in the lane. On a cargo bike's basket rail that's a true 3 feet; center-mounted on a rack, it's 4.

Lit the whole way

LEDs wrapped along the pole, sealed in heat shrink. At night it reads as a glowing saber, and riders report being visible for miles.

One idea, two builds

V1 hangs the pole on a flipped kickstand hinge, drilled and bent by hand. V2 prints the hinge instead, so it just assembles. Both swing the same pole out to the same line. The two versions are split out below.

The pole end sits where a car's mirror would have to cross. Drivers move over on their own.

Why it exists: the V1 story

LaneSaber started in Santa Cruz, California, after its inventor, Abe, was in three bike-car accidents in a single year, and then watched a driver nearly hit a child on a BikeBus ride. He built the first one out of a kickstand, a fiberglass pole, and LEDs, in the spirit of the pool noodles cycle tourists strap to their racks, but visible, legal, and lit. That first build became V1, the metal original. In the 18 months after he started riding with it: not one incident. It's an interim fix. The real answer is better roads, but until those exist, it gives riders some control back, and a little peace of mind.

"You can see her for miles. It lit up the whole road."

Neighbors of Nancy Spoolman, LaneSaber trike rider, Rapid City, SD

Riding to Crescent City, just north of Leggett, a logging truck hit Taylor Nichols' LaneSaber and took the end piece clean off, on a no-shoulder section, without slowing down. The pole took the hit. Taylor didn't.

Taylor said it scared him, and may have saved his life

LaneSaber was given away on day one and stays that way: open source, community-driven, no permission needed. The hope is that local builders and bike co-ops make them for their own towns instead of one shop shipping them around the world. About 30 are on the road today, and every new one makes the next driver's education a little easier.

Two versions. One line.

LaneSaber comes in two generations, and they are kept separate on this page on purpose. V1 is the metal original, the one from the story above: a flipped kickstand hinge, drilled and bent by hand, about $50 in parts. V2 is the 3D printed redesign: no kickstand, no drilling, no bending. Print the pieces and assemble them. Same pole, same lit 3-foot line, a much easier build.

V1 · Metal · The original

V1: the metal original

The workshop build. A wall kickstand flipped upside down becomes the hinge, the pole clamps on, LEDs wrap the pole, heat shrink seals it. Three years of road testing and about 30 riders stand behind this one. It is also heavy, clunky, and asks for tools and patience.

  • Kickstand hinge, drilled and bent by hand
  • About $50 in parts at real prices
  • Full build free on Instructables
  • The version in the story and the photos above
See the V1 build
V2 · 3D printed · The new one

V2: print and assemble

The redesign. The metal hinge is replaced by printed parts that snap and bolt together, so the workshop steps are gone. Print the pieces at home, at a library, or at a makerspace, sand the edges, assemble, wrap the pole, seal it. Lighter, cheaper to kit, and far easier to teach.

  • No kickstand, no drilling, no bending
  • Print, sand, assemble: that is the whole build
  • Files free; kit starts at $40
  • Same 3-foot reach, same LED wrap
See the V2 build

Where the money goes: V1, the metal one

This is an anti-capitalist project, so the books are open. Actual parts cost of one metal V1, at the prices Abe actually pays:

Kickstand (the hinge)$12
LED strip (Amazon)$15
Heat shrink$10
Fiberglass pole~$5
Clamps and hardware$2
Tape, flag bits, connectors~$6
Parts totalabout $50

That is parts only, before the drilling, bending, wrapping, and sealing time V1 takes. Removing that labor is the whole point of V2. Prices cover parts, build time, packaging, and keeping the project alive, not profit maximization. If the price is the barrier, build it yourself for parts cost, or ask your local bike co-op to run a build night. Nobody should skip being seen because of money.

The build, in short: V1 vs V2

Same jobs, two very different workshops. V1 is metal and hands-on. V2 is print and assemble. The full V1 build with every photo lives on Instructables; the V2 print and assembly sheet comes with the free files.

V1, metal: the workshop build

Flip a kickstand

Mount a wall kickstand upside down on the rear rack. That spring hinge is the whole mechanism, vertical to horizontal in one motion.

Drill and bend

Drill the hinge plate and bend the kickstand to fit the rack. This is the fussy, tool-heavy part, and it is exactly what V2 removes.

Fit the pole

Clamp a fiberglass pole to the hinge. 3 feet of reach from a cargo basket rail, 4 feet from a center rack mount.

Wrap the LEDs, then seal

Spiral the LED strip along the pole, wire it to a USB battery pack, add flag or tape at the end, then heat-shrink over the wrap to waterproof it. Soft rubber cap on the end.

Full 8-step V1 build on Instructables

V2, printed: print and assemble

Print the pieces

Print the mount set, pole clamp, and end cap from the free files. Your printer, a neighbor's, the library's, a makerspace's: all fine.

Sand and test-fit

Knock down the rough edges and test-fit the pieces. A few minutes with sandpaper. No power tools, no drill press.

Assemble

Snap and bolt the printed hinge together on the rack and clamp the pole in. No kickstand, no drilling, no bending.

Wrap the LEDs, then seal

Same finish as V1: spiral the LEDs along the pole, wire to a USB battery pack, heat-shrink over the top, soft cap on the end. Go ride.

Why V2 exists

V1 proved the idea on the road. V2 removes every step that needed a workshop, so a rider, a family, or a whole bike co-op can build one on a kitchen table. The metal original is not going anywhere; its plans stay free and its story stays at the top of this page.

Get the free V2 print files

Finding a pole (it's easier than you think)

The pole is the bulkiest part to ship and the easiest to find locally. It is the same fiberglass rod sold as a driveway marker for plowing snow-country roads. Hardware stores stock them for about $5, and Amazon sells multipacks of reflective driveway markers that split perfectly between a whole bike club. Source it locally, and the kit gets cheaper, smaller, and faster. That's by design: poles should come from your town, not a parcel from California.

V2 plans and 3D print files, free

Free means free: no account, no paywall, no "premium version." Print the pieces on any 3D printer: yours, a neighbor's, your local library's, a makerspace's. The files are being finalized against the current V2 mount design and will download from right here; until they land, the V1 metal build on Instructables is the complete free path, live now.

Co-ops, bike kitchens, clubs: build them there

The model is local builders making LaneSabers for their own area: no license, no royalty, no permission needed, no need to report back. Run a build night, sell them at cost, give them away. If you want a hand, Abe will walk your crew through the build over Zoom or Google Meet, and kits or a sample can come through the Etsy shop. One LaneSaber on a bike in your town starts doing the outreach by itself.

Questions

What is the difference between V1 and V2?

V1 is the original metal build: a flipped kickstand hinge, drilled and bent by hand, about $50 in parts, documented free on Instructables. V2 is the 3D printed redesign: no kickstand, no drilling, no bending, just print and assemble. Same pole, same LED wrap, same 3-foot line.

What powers it?

A USB battery pack you supply (the Etsy listing spells out the current options). The battery isn't included so the kit stays small and cheap to ship. Most riders already own a power bank.

What bikes does it fit?

Anything with a rear rack. Commuters, cargo bikes, and family haulers are the sweet spot. Low riders benefit most: trikes, recumbents, and handcycles sit below the sightline of today's tall cars, and a pole above car height makes them visible. Adaptive groups are very welcome to get in touch about mounting.

Is it safe if a car hits it?

That's the design brief. The end is soft and rubber-covered, the fiberglass pole flexes, and under a hard hit it snaps rather than spearing or dragging the rider. When a logging truck clipped Taylor Nichols' LaneSaber, the pole gave its life and Taylor kept his.

Can I sell LaneSabers I build?

Yes. It's open source and community-driven on purpose. Build them for your area and sell them locally. All that's asked is that you keep them affordable and keep riders safe.

What about shipping outside the US?

International shipping is genuinely painful and expensive, which is exactly why the design is free and the pole is sourced locally. If you're outside the US, the build path is the intended path, and remote build help is free.
